title: A 90-day personal branding plan for doctors, lawyers, CAs and consultants
metaDescription: A 90-day personal branding plan for doctors, lawyers, CAs and consultants in India, with the advertising limits regulators set and how to stay within them.
lead: Professionals win work on trust, and trust now often starts with a search of your name. But doctors, advocates and chartered accountants in India work under advertising rules that most branding advice ignores. This plan builds visibility over 90 days by teaching rather than selling, and keeps you on the right side of your regulator.
keyPoints: Check your regulator's current rules before you post: the NMC, the Bar Council of India and ICAI each limit promotion differently.
Education is the safest and most effective content for regulated professionals.
Spend the first 30 days on positioning, profiles and a bank of questions, not on posting volume.
Measure referrals, invitations and the quality of inquiries rather than followers.

sections.heading: Why professionals need a different playbook
paragraphs: A consumer brand can shout. A cardiologist, a tax advocate or a CA can't, and shouldn't want to. Their clients are buying judgment, and the content that builds a reputation for judgment is careful, specific and useful: explaining a condition, a legal process or a tax change more clearly than anyone else nearby.

Then there is the regulator. Several Indian professions have rules that limit self-promotion, solicitation and testimonials. Those rules don't rule out a personal brand; they define the lane it runs in. Inside that lane, education, informed opinion and visible expertise are generally welcome.

sections.heading: Know your regulator's limits first
paragraphs: Rules change, and the summaries below are a starting point, not legal advice. Read the current text from your regulator or professional body, and ask them or a lawyer whenever a specific post feels unclear.
bullets: **Doctors:** on 6 October 2026 the National Medical Commission issued Guidelines on Ethical Advertising and Public Communication for hospitals and registered medical practitioners, effective immediately. As reported, they bar promotional use of patient testimonials and before-and-after photos, superlatives such as 'best doctor', promises of a cure, paid rankings, fake reviews or followers, and using influencers or other third parties to do indirectly what a doctor cannot do directly. Factual health education without promotional intent remains permitted, and AI-generated content that is allowed must state that it came from AI.

**Advocates:** Rule 36 of the Bar Council of India Rules bars advocates from soliciting work or advertising, directly or indirectly. A 2008 amendment allows a website carrying limited factual particulars such as name, contact details and enrollment information. Anything that reads as a pitch for work is risky.

**Chartered accountants:** ICAI's revised Code of Ethics, 13th edition, applies from 1 April 2026 and relaxes parts of the advertisement and website guidelines — for example, members may now promote services that aren't exclusive to the profession. Limits on solicitation remain, so read the Code's advertisement guidelines before running ads or promotional posts.

**Consultants and other advisers:** many consultants answer to no professional body, but ASCI's code still applies to their advertising, and ASCI expects anyone giving stock or investment advice on social media to be SEBI-registered and to say so upfront.

sections.heading: Days 1–30: foundations
paragraphs: The first month is about clarity, not output. Write a one-line positioning statement: who you help, with what, and what is distinctive about your approach. 'Pediatric allergist helping Pune parents make sense of food allergies' works. So does 'CA helping Delhi startups stay GST-compliant through their first funding round'.
bullets: Choose one primary platform. LinkedIn suits CAs, lawyers and B2B consultants; Instagram and YouTube suit doctors explaining health to the public.
Update every profile with the same photo, positioning line and accurate credentials, and complete your Google Business Profile if you run a practice.
Write a compliance checklist for your profession and keep it next to your drafts.
Build a content bank: list 30 questions clients or patients ask, and the misconceptions you correct every week.
Set a cadence you can keep. Two posts a week is plenty to start.

sections.heading: Days 31–60: publish, listen and adjust
paragraphs: Start publishing from the content bank and mix formats: a short explainer post, a carousel or document that walks through a process, and now and then a video of you answering one question. Video shows how you think and speak better than any other format, which is exactly what a prospective client wants to know.

Listen as much as you post. Note which topics draw thoughtful comments, saves and messages from the people you serve. Reply generously, but don't give individual advice in public; move personal cases to a proper consultation. Comment on posts by peers, journalists and institutions in your field, because being visible in those conversations builds credibility faster than posting alone.

This is also the moment to accept talks, panels and guest articles. India's medical ethics code has long drawn the line here in a useful way: doctors may write and speak on public health, but not in a manner that advertises themselves. The same spirit serves every profession.

sections.heading: Days 61–90: compound what works
paragraphs: By the third month you have data on what your audience values. Use it to build assets that keep working after the 90 days end.
bullets: Turn your three strongest topics into one evergreen piece: a guide on your website, a long-form video or a newsletter edition.
Start a monthly update for clients and referrers, sent only to people who opted in.
Collaborate with adjacent professionals — a CA and a lawyer explaining a new compliance rule together, or a physiotherapist and an orthopedic surgeon on recovery myths.
Search your own name, review the first page of results and fix anything outdated.
Plan the next quarter around what drew the right audience, not the biggest one.

sections.heading: Content that educates without soliciting
paragraphs: The most dependable formula is a common question, a clear answer and the context a layperson needs. Some starting points by profession:
bullets: **Doctors:** when a symptom needs a specialist, myths versus evidence, how to prepare for a procedure, how to read a common test report.
**Advocates:** how a process works step by step, what a new law or judgment means in general terms, which documents to keep ready — without inviting readers to hire you.
**CAs:** filing calendars, plain explanations of tax or GST changes, common errors in small-business books.
**Consultants:** the frameworks you use, anonymized lessons from projects, teardowns of public examples in your industry.

sections.heading: A pre-publish compliance check
paragraphs: Notice what the content ideas above leave out: named client outcomes, patient stories, 'book now' offers and comparisons with rivals. For regulated professionals, those are the elements most likely to cross a line. Run every draft through a short check before it goes out, and rewrite or ask when any answer is uncertain.
bullets: No patient or client can be identified, directly or from context.
No promise of results, cures or case outcomes.
No superlatives, rankings or awards you can't independently verify.
Qualifications and registration details are accurate and current.
AI-assisted images, video or text are disclosed where your regulator or ASCI expects it.
No paid boosts unless your regulator's current rules clearly allow them.
You would be comfortable with your professional body reading the post aloud.

sections.heading: Measure reputation, not reach
paragraphs: Follower counts mean little for a professional practice. Track the signals that predict work: referrals from other professionals, invitations to speak or write, the quality of inquiries, newsletter sign-ups and what appears when someone searches your name. Record a baseline on day one and compare on day 90.

If you'd like a team to help with positioning, content and compliance checks, our [personal branding](/personal-branding) service is built for this, and the [personal branding guide](/personal-branding/guide) explains the method in more detail. Clinics can also see how we approach [healthcare and wellness](/industries/healthcare-wellness) marketing, and professionals focused on LinkedIn may find our [LinkedIn thought leadership guide](/insights/linkedin-thought-leadership-founders) useful.

faqs.q: Can doctors in India run social media ads?
faqs.a: Proceed with great care. The NMC's October 2026 guidelines restrict promotional advertising by doctors, including inducements, testimonials and paid rankings, while allowing factual health education. Read the full NMC text and check with your State Medical Council before spending on any promotion.

Many share general legal information and commentary. The line to avoid is solicitation — content that invites readers to hire you or advertises your services. Check the Bar Council of India Rules and your State Bar Council's guidance.

faqs.q: Should a professional use a ghostwriter?
faqs.a: A writer can help shape and edit, but the expertise and opinions must be yours, and you remain responsible for every claim. Regulators hold the professional accountable, not the agency.

faqs.q: How much time does this plan take each week?
faqs.a: Roughly two to four hours: time to draft, time to record or review, and short daily sessions to reply and comment. Batching content once a week keeps it manageable alongside a full practice.
